stories.headline: Update: Ethiopia-Tigray War Resumes as Army Confirms Fighting, Airports Seized
stories.summary:
Ethiopia's army issued its first official statement Thursday confirming active fighting with Tigrayan forces, saying it has repelled attacks in the Amhara region near the Tigray border and inflicted heavy casualties. The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) had seized control of three airports from federal police on Wednesday, and the TPLF's vice-president was quoted by AFP saying: "We are in the situation of full-blown war now." Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.

The escalation follows months of mounting tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government and Tigrayan authorities, who fought a devastating civil war from 2020 to 2022. That conflict, which ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal, is estimated to have killed approximately 600,000 people and pushed the region to the brink of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced a new alliance with six other armed groups aimed at ousting the government.

Unconfirmed reports indicate TPLF forces have also launched artillery attacks in the neighboring Afar region, targeting the town of Yallo near the Tigray border. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle describe the city itself as calm but economically devastated, with civil servants going unpaid and banks running out of cash for months. The BBC is unable to independently verify military claims from either side and cannot report directly from the region.

This is a significant new development on a previously covered story: where earlier reporting noted mutual accusations and fears of resumed war, the Ethiopian army has now confirmed active combat operations, the TPLF has physically seized federal infrastructure, and a senior Tigrayan official has declared full-blown war.

stories.headline: Energy Secretary Wright Breaks With White House Over Proposed Diesel Export Ban
stories.summary:
Energy Secretary Chris Wright publicly broke with President Trump on Wednesday, arguing that a proposed 90-day ban on U.S. diesel exports would backfire and push fuel prices higher rather than lower them. Speaking at a Climate Week event hosted by the New York Times in New York, Wright said: "The blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn't work," warning that forcing refineries to cut output would put "upward pressure on gasoline prices and jet fuel prices." The White House has been reported to be working on a 90-day export ban in response to diesel prices that have reached all-time highs.

Fuel analysts backed Wright's assessment. GasBuddy analyst Patrick De Haan warned that a ban could raise gasoline prices toward record levels, as cutting diesel output would hit gasoline production hardest. Wright acknowledged the administration would make a formal policy announcement later in the week, saying any action would not be a "black and white" halt to diesel exports but would focus on increasing domestic supply and ensuring refineries run at full capacity.

The public split between Wright and the White House reflects broader tension within the administration over how to respond to elevated energy prices. The U.S. currently exports approximately 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day, making the policy question consequential for both domestic consumers and global energy markets. Supporters of a ban argue it would provide near-term relief for American truckers and industries dependent on diesel; critics say any short-term benefit would be overwhelmed by longer-term price distortions.

The story is covered by 22 outlets across the political spectrum, making it one of the most broadly tracked domestic policy stories of the day. A formal White House announcement is expected before the end of the week.

stories.headline: Poland Says Fire at Starlink Station Is Russian Sabotage; Denmark Warns of Growing Military Threat
stories.summary:
Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski declared Thursday that a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage," saying it was "deliberately designed to disable the station" and disrupt internet access for Ukrainian military users. The station, located in the Masovian Voivodeship, remains operational. Gawkowski said multiple indications suggest the attack fits into what he called "a new Russian doctrine of attack," though the Kremlin has not commented. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the incident "looks bad" while stopping short of a definitive attribution.

The sabotage announcement came on the same day Poland reported a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing it to scramble fighter jets — an incident already reported Wednesday. Denmark's intelligence service simultaneously issued a new threat assessment warning of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against NATO countries, while expecting Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months.

The incidents fit a broader pattern across Europe: Germany recently blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, and France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure. Hybrid warfare tactics — including cyberattacks, sabotage, and misinformation — have been increasingly attributed to Russia across the continent, though Moscow consistently denies involvement. Russian President Putin has repeatedly stated Moscow does not plan to attack NATO states.

Separately, Russian overnight strikes on Ukraine's Kharkiv region killed six people and injured twelve in a strike on a farm, as the broader conflict continues.

stories.headline: Houthis Fire Six Ballistic Missiles at Saudi Cities; Kingdom Says All Intercepted
stories.summary:
Saudi Arabia's military said Thursday it intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Houthi militia toward the Red Sea port city of Yanbu and the inland city of Taif. The Iran-backed Houthis did not immediately claim responsibility for the attack, and there were no immediate reports of casualties or significant damage. The Saudi military did not provide details on the interception systems used.

The strikes represent a fresh escalation in Houthi attacks on Saudi territory, occurring in the context of the broader U.S.-Iran conflict and continued instability in the Red Sea region. The Houthis have maintained an intermittent campaign of missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia and regional shipping, actions they say are in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. The attacks on Yanbu and Taif — cities well inside Saudi territory — signal the Houthis' continued capacity to strike civilian and economic infrastructure far from Yemen's borders.

The incident adds regional pressure at a moment when the United Nations General Assembly is convening in New York, where the Iran conflict and Middle East stability are central agenda items. Saudi Arabia has not commented on any retaliatory measures.

stories.headline: Update: Xi Jinping Arrives in Washington for State Visit; U.S.-China Trade Truce Extended Two Months
stories.summary:
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington Wednesday evening for his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade, greeted by President Trump in an unusual tarmac welcome at Joint Base Andrews — a diplomatic gesture that departed from the standard White House arrival protocol. The visit marks a significant moment in U.S.-China relations following a prolonged period of trade tensions and geopolitical friction.

Coinciding with Xi's arrival, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two countries have agreed to extend their existing trade truce for two months, through January 10. The so-called Busan Agreement had paused hostilities in the trade war between the world's two largest economies. Key issues expected to dominate the summit include trade, Taiwan, artificial intelligence, and climate policy.

The state visit comes amid a backdrop of ongoing U.S. military engagement with Iran, global supply chain pressures, and broader questions about the strategic rivalry between Washington and Beijing. Analysts note that Trump's tarmac welcome and the trade truce extension signal a desire by both sides to stabilize the relationship, at least in the near term.

The scope of any longer-term agreements remains unclear, with observers noting that Trump has not publicly articulated specific goals for the summit beyond broad economic and security interests.

stories.headline: Update: U.S.-Iran War Continues as Both Sides Meet at UN; Pentagon Warns of Munitions Shortfalls
stories.summary:
The U.S.-Iran conflict continued to dominate global attention this week as both sides held their first direct talks since a ceasefire collapsed in June, meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian delivered a defiant address to the UN General Assembly, rejecting U.S. terms, even as President Trump warned he would 'annihilate' Iran if a peace deal is not reached.

The Pentagon's inspector general issued a significant new warning, finding that Operation Epic Fury has created 'shortfalls' in U.S. munitions stockpiles and a bottleneck in resupply chains — directly contradicting Trump's public assertions that American military supplies are 'virtually limitless.' The findings raise questions about U.S. military readiness if the conflict escalates or drags on.

Images obtained by CBS News showed widespread damage to multiple U.S. installations in the Middle East from Iranian strikes. Iran and the U.S. also traded conflicting accounts over the status of an oil tanker, El Gaia, with Tehran claiming it caught fire after hitting mines and Washington asserting it was struck by a missile and drone.

The diplomatic and military situation remains fluid. Neither side has articulated a clear exit strategy, analysts note, and the intermittent exchange of fire since June has yet to produce conditions for a durable ceasefire. The war has also begun driving up global energy prices, with particular impact on diesel costs in the United States.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky Says U.S. Pushing Energy Ceasefire, Black Sea Corridor, and Trilateral Talks with Russia
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios in an interview Wednesday that the Trump administration is pressing for three immediate de-escalation steps in the Russia-Ukraine war: a ceasefire on energy infrastructure, the reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and a trilateral U.S.-Russia-Ukraine meeting, possibly to be held in Abu Dhabi.

The disclosure represents the clearest public articulation to date of the Trump administration's near-term diplomatic priorities for the conflict. Trump has signaled renewed interest in restarting a diplomatic track after earlier peace efforts stalled, though Russian officials have not publicly confirmed acceptance of any of the proposed steps.

The proposed energy ceasefire would halt strikes on power grids and fuel infrastructure, which have caused significant civilian hardship in Ukraine during the war. Reopening the Black Sea corridor would allow Ukrainian grain exports to resume, a matter of significant consequence for global food supplies and developing-world food security.

Separately, the first North Korean soldiers captured alive since Pyongyang joined Russia's war effort in 2024 have been apprehended, with President Zelensky criticizing North Korea for using its citizens as 'currency' to support Russia.

stories.headline: Pakistan Strikes Afghanistan After Accusing Kabul of Cross-Border Drone Attacks
stories.summary:
Pakistan announced Wednesday that it had conducted aerial and drone strikes against ten locations in Afghanistan's southeastern Khost province, accusing the Taliban-led government in Kabul of launching drone attacks inside Pakistani territory. Pakistan said its forces thwarted the Afghan-originated attacks before retaliating. Afghan officials said the Pakistani strikes caused no casualties.

The strikes mark a significant escalation in longstanding tensions between Islamabad and Kabul, which have frequently traded accusations over cross-border militant activity and airspace violations since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. Pakistan has repeatedly blamed Afghan soil for sheltering militant groups responsible for attacks inside Pakistan.

The Taliban government in Kabul has consistently denied harboring anti-Pakistan militants and has rejected Pakistani military operations on Afghan territory as violations of sovereignty. The latest exchange raises concerns about a broader destabilization of the region at a time when both countries face significant internal pressures.

The incident has drawn limited international comment so far, though it comes amid an already complex security environment in South Asia and could further strain Pakistan's fraught relationship with its western neighbor.
